column2: To understand a work as one's own is to recognize which work is one's own and to grasp, as far as one can see, what it is and what it does; one who suspects a work is theirs and refuses to find out is not excused by that refusal.
To remain turned away from something is to hold a turning from it, rather than toward it, as a standing over time, and not to be in the course of turning back.
To stand turned toward something is to hold a turning toward it as a standing over time, which persists without continuous attention to it.
The contrary of a standing is a standing that cannot hold together with it in the same subject, toward the same object, at the same time, though both can be absent.
To hold a work as one's own is to acknowledge oneself as its author, inwardly or in speech, rather than to disown it or lay it on another.
To take a work for what it is is to take it by its character as far as one can see it, right or wrong, rather than by a flattering cover or by a condemnation of the person in place of the deed.
